doc.title: Toots Thielemans — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Goodman and Shearing as integration pioneers
summary: They discuss mixed bands and why race did not affect Toots.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, ‘cause I was just wondering, you know, because maybe in your… back in the ’50s, they didn’t know that America was two separate because you can’t see it on the records.
[laughs]
No, no.
You know. So I was just… But perhaps because of the…
That’s, that’s… Well, Benny Goodman was the first one with Lionel Hampton, right?
Mm-hmm. And Teddy Wilson.
And Charlie Christian.
And Charlie Christian and then Ted--
And…
Teddy Wilson.
Teddy Wilson, mm-hmm. And in the ’50s, George Shearing.
Mm-hmm.
You know? He didn’t… Well, I’m blind. I don’t know what, know what those are. Life approaches the dramatic subject, you know. But yeah.
It didn’t affect you, though. Or maybe…

No, because I was, to me… the music was so important and my sense of humor, my sense of being was so much… You’ve met me, right? I mean, I haven’t changed, and I was like that when I came to this country and I was looking for and I enjoyed the group with Shearing was a mixed group in those days. Like two black guys, right? Milt, Clark. And McKibbon and me and the English fella, [inaudible]. [laughs] Yeah.
Yeah. So, but you know, now that America is much different, you know, but some people…
Yeah.
We have to remember that things were different in the past.
Yes, [it was?].
And maybe the music helped make it different because, like you say, Benny Goodman…
Goodman.
George Shearing and… so pioneers—people who were charting new territory.
They were pioneers, right. I must say, I wasn’t that, you know… of course I didn’t go militantly. I should have, maybe.
Maybe it wasn’t necessary. The statement was made…
Yeah.
…by the camaraderie on stage and people could see…
Yes, certainly.
